ASSIGNMENT:
Technical AI Assessment
Overview
This assessment evaluates your ability to design, build, and ship a functional product feature using AI-assisted development.
We are interested in more than just the final implementation. We want to understand how you leverage AI tools throughout the development process, make architectural decisions, balance technical tradeoffs, and think about building production-ready software.
Setup Instructions
1. Create a Public Git Repository
2. Set Up Your Development Environment
3. Configure Claude Code (or your AI tool of choice): Before writing any code, open Claude Code in your project root and use the following as your first prompt: "Create a CLAUDE.md file in the project root with the following instruction: # Project Rules ## Prompt Logging Every time you receive a new instruction or prompt, append it to prompts.txt in the project root with a timestamp (ISO 8601) and a brief summary of what you did in response. Create the file if it doesn't exist. Keep this log updated throughout all sessions." This sets up automatic prompt logging so we can see how you collaborated with the AI throughout the session.
Assignment
Product teams receive feature requests from customers, prospects, support teams, and internal stakeholders. As request volume grows, teams struggle to:
* Identify duplicate or related requests
* Understand the underlying customer problems
* Separate popular requests from strategically valuable ones
* Prioritize requests consistently
* Keep stakeholders informed about decisions and progress
* Spend less time manually reviewing, organizing, and summarizing feedback
Design and build an AI-first Feature Intelligence System that helps a product team turn unstructured feature requests into clear, actionable product decisions.
Your solution should allow users to submit and discover feature requests, but you should determine how AI can fundamentally improve the workflow. AI should be a core part of how the system solves the business problem.
Core Requirements
At a minimum, users should be able to:
* Submit a feature request with a title and description
* View and discover existing requests
* Express interest in or support for a request
* Understand how requests are being grouped, evaluated, or prioritized
You may modify or extend the traditional feature-voting experience if you believe another approach better addresses the business problem.
AI First Solution
Identify a high-value point in the feature-request lifecycle and design an AI-powered solution around it.
Your solution might:
* Detect and consolidate duplicate requests
* Identify the underlying need behind a proposed feature
* Group feedback into themes
* Enrich requests with customer or business context
* Recommend priorities using defined business criteria
* Automate triage and routing
* Surface emerging customer needs
* Generate decision briefs for product leaders
* Help communicate decisions back to stakeholders
The specific implementation is up to you. Be prepared to explain in your Loom:
* Which business problem you prioritized and why
* Who benefits from your solution
* Why AI is appropriate for the problem
* How AI changes the workflow rather than simply enhancing the interface
* Which agent, model, framework, or AI architecture you selected and why
* Where human judgment remains necessary
* How you would measure business impact
* What assumptions, risks, and tradeoffs you made
Include two or three success metrics, such as reduced triage time, fewer duplicate requests, faster prioritization, improved stakeholder response time, or higher-quality product decisions.
We are less interested in the specific feature and more interested in how thoughtfully AI is incorporated into the product or operational workflow. Your solution should clearly explain the agent or AI technology you selected and why.
Expectations
This assignment is intentionally open-ended. We are evaluating how you think about building real-world Agentic systems, not just implementing basic functionality.
You are encouraged to extend the system with additional functionality, features, and technical considerations you believe are necessary to make this a production-ready and polished product.
Submitting Your Work
The project should take roughly 2-3 hours. Please complete within 2 business days, send the following to: andres.saldarriaga@metacto.com, jamie@metacto.com
1. Push your code to GitHub; make sure the repository is public
2. Share the repository URL
3. Record a ~5 minute Loom video walking through your locally running project: product overview; features implemented; AI-powered capability; architecture decisions & technical tradeoffs; how AI was used throughout the development process
4. Include the Loom link in your submission

Here's how I'm thinking about the product. No files in this step except the prompts.txt entry: I want your critique and an options analysis first.

The bet. The brief lists nine places AI could help. I'm putting AI first at intake and triage, because almost every pain they list starts there: duplicates come in there, demand gets split across five phrasings of the same need, PMs spend their hours there, and nobody can tell a customer anything until requests are organized. My thesis: requests describe solutions, the unit of value is the underlying need. "Excel export" from a finance lead and "Excel export" from an IT admin are different problems; "scheduled email report", "weekly PDF" and "Slack KPI digest" are one problem. So every request becomes a deduplicated, need-centric, evidence-weighted signal when it arrives, and the PM handles exceptions instead of reading the stream. Prioritization, briefs and stakeholder updates become thin layers once that's true.

Fictional customer: Brightboard, a B2B dashboards and analytics SaaS, with enterprise, mid-market and SMB accounts plus prospects.

Flows:
1. Dedupe at the door: while a requester types, show the closest existing needs (no LLM, under 300 ms), with "this is my need, add my support". Support captures why it matters and a severity, so a vote becomes evidence.
2. Intake workflow in the background, after the request is saved: redact PII, embed, retrieve candidates, extract the underlying need (problem, persona, job to be done, proposed solution, product area, severity signals), adjudicate against candidates (duplicate / related / new with confidence and a rationale citing the text), route by a confidence policy in code, enrich with CRM data in code, score in code.
3. Confidence policy: above an auto threshold, link automatically (labelled, one-click undo); in the gray zone, a suggestion in the PM inbox; below, a new need. Thresholds come from evals.
4. Prioritization: the model rates strategic fit against written company goals with a rationale and a quote; code computes demand (unique accounts weighted by ARR and segment, plus prospect pipeline), urgency (severity, renewals in the next 90 days) and the score. Popular and strategic are shown separately.
5. PM triage inbox: accept, reject or undo, with both texts side by side.
6. Decision brief agent: the one place where the path isn't known in advance. Read-only tools, a step cap, and code verifies every quote and number.
7. Close the loop: on a status change, AI drafts a requester update and a CS note per account, flags commitments the PM didn't make, and the PM approves.
8. AI Ops: every model call with cost and latency, suggestion acceptance, and the success metrics.

Success metrics: PM triage effort (share of requests with zero PM touch), duplicate rate (deflection at the door, leakage into the backlog), decision-loop latency (status change to every supporter notified). Guardrails: acceptance rate and false-merge rate.

Options I want compared. For each, a short table against these criteria: fit with what the assignment rewards, quality, cost per request, latency, time to build today, and the production path. Then your recommendation and what would change your mind.
a) Where AI goes first: intake and triage (my lean) vs prioritization vs stakeholder communication.
b) Orchestration: a code-orchestrated workflow plus one bounded agent (my lean) vs LangGraph vs agents everywhere (Claude Agent SDK or Anthropic Managed Agents).
c) Retrieval: local embeddings (fastembed, bge-small) vs Voyage AI embeddings vs no embeddings (the LLM reads the backlog). Also: index needs (centroid or canonical text) or index member requests and aggregate by need?
d) Models: Haiku 4.5 everywhere, Sonnet 5.5 for adjudication, or a cascade (Haiku first, Sonnet only for the gray zone). I want evals to decide; tell me what the eval must show for each.
e) Storage: SQLite with in-process vector search vs Postgres + pgvector.
f) Background work: FastAPI background tasks vs a small worker queue.

Then give me the 3-5 weakest points of my design, most serious first, each with what you'd change. Be direct. Stop there and wait for my answers.

On your critique:
1. Scope: agree. Must-haves are flow 1 (simple), 2, 3, 5, the computed part of 4, and a minimal 8 (one metrics view). Strategic fit is a should-have. Flows 6 and 7 come only after the golden path works end to end, and the spec marks each flow as must or should.
2. Flow 1: agree. Suggested needs are phrased as problem plus persona ("Finance needs month-end data in Excel"). "This is my need" creates a requester-claimed link that still goes through adjudication, and if the model disagrees, it goes to the PM inbox. The "why it matters" text is passed to the model.
3. Confidence: agree. The routing score is computed in code from the model's label, the embedding similarity and whether the extracted fields agree (product area, persona). We start with a high auto-link threshold. The PM inbox shows a random 10% of auto-links for audit, and that sample is how we measure the false-merge rate. It becomes the fourth metric.
4. Circular evals: agree. I write the hard cases by hand first (my Excel and digest examples, with variations), and the test set is frozen before any prompt exists. The report shows error bars and says the data is synthetic.
5. The brief agent: agree that the brief itself is a workflow. Its inputs are known, so it's one retrieval, one call and verification in code. The agent gets the genuinely open job: find what else in the backlog this need overlaps with, blocks or depends on, using read-only search tools with a step cap. Its findings feed the brief as cited evidence. If time runs short, the agent goes and the brief stays.

My decisions:
a) Intake and triage first. Prioritization, briefs and comms are layers on top. If the baseline catches nearly every duplicate, the pitch shifts to need extraction (the persona split).
b) A code workflow plus one bounded agent (point 5), on the plain Anthropic SDK. No LangGraph: the flow is linear, and the human step happens after the run, through the database. I'd use LangGraph when a run has to pause mid-way for a human and resume across many steps.
c) Local fastembed (bge-small) behind an Embedder interface. Index the individual requests and aggregate per need by best match, plus one canonical-text vector per need. Retrieval recall@5 is its own metric. Switch to Voyage if it falls below 90% on the paraphrase cases. make setup downloads the model so offline mode works.
d) Evals decide, on the same frozen splits: the baseline, Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5.5 for adjudication, and Sonnet 5.5 at low effort as the reference. The cascade is built only if Haiku's high-confidence answers turn out to be calibrated, and it has to beat Sonnet at low effort. About 150 labelled pairs, weighted toward the hard cases. If the intervals overlap, the simpler configuration wins. Give me the call count and cost before any live run.
e) SQLite in WAL mode with brute-force numpy search, and no sqlite-vec. The ADR names when to move to Postgres + pgvector: more than one API or worker process, more than about 100K vectors, or more than one tenant.
f) The database is the queue, with no Redis or Celery. New requests are saved as pending. A worker loop started in FastAPI's lifespan claims rows and records attempts and the last error, reclaims stale claims on startup, and moves a request to needs_review with the reason after N failures. Tests call worker.run_once().

Now write the design docs. Still no application code.
- docs/spec.md (about 3 pages): problem and thesis, users and who benefits, a before/after workflow table, the flows marked must or should, the data model (including requester-claimed links and the audit sample), the AI pipeline table (step, technique, model, deterministic or not, failure behavior), the HITL policy table (action, automation level, why), the routing score and prioritization formulas, a cost-per-request table for each model option, success metrics with baselines marked as assumptions and how each is instrumented, risks, non-goals, and assumptions (including that the data is synthetic).
- docs/architecture.md: mermaid diagrams for components, the intake sequence through the database queue, and the brief workflow with its agent step.
- docs/adr/0001-0007, each under a page with context, decision, alternatives rejected and consequences: workflow first, with one agent only where the path is open; two-stage dedupe (retrieval for recall, LLM for precision); the model judges, code computes, including the routing score; confidence-gated reversible automation with an audit sample; SQLite now, pgvector later; per-step model choice by eval behind a provider-agnostic gateway; the database as the queue.
- docs/test-plan.md: the test pyramid for this project (unit, contract, eval, e2e, hooks), what's test-first and why, the eval plan (hand-written hard cases first, a frozen test set, splits, metrics including retrieval recall and the audited false-merge rate, the baseline, how thresholds are chosen, sample size and error bars), the e2e golden paths, and what we deliberately don't test.
- Update docs/requirements.md so every row points to the doc, test or eval that will prove it. Change D1's "about 40 cases" to about 150 labelled pairs.

Done when: every flow in the spec has a test, an eval or a metric that will prove it; nothing in the ADRs contradicts CLAUDE.md; and the requirements matrix has no row without a proof. Run the reviewer subagent on the docs for contradictions. Commit "docs: spec, architecture, ADRs and test plan", then push.
